About this document


This document provides the teaching content for Music Years 11–13 of the
New Zealand Curriculum.

Progress and assessment information for Music Years 11–13 is still in development.
Once that is completed, Music Years 11–13 is proposed to be made by the Minister of
Education as a National Curriculum Statement under section 90(1)(a) of the
Education and Training Act 2020.

It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Music Years 11–13 will be required to start using it in Year 11 from
1 January 2028, in Year 12 from 1 January 2029, and in Year 13 from 1 January
2030.

This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.

  In Music, students are taught analytical, compositional, and performance-based                   Music leads to pathways in performance, composition, musicology, music
  knowledge and practices, alongside the use of contemporary music technologies.                   education, and related areas such as music therapy.
  Through the teaching of a diverse range of musical traditions, styles, and genres,
  students broaden their knowledge of music as both an art form and a means of
  cultural expression. Students are taught how to refine their musical abilities and
  develop frameworks for interpreting and responding to the world through music,
  informed by both theory and practice.

Students are taught the core concepts that underpin music as a creative,
performative, and cultural discipline. This includes how music is organised through
elements such as rhythm, melody, harmony, and texture and how musical ideas are
represented and communicated. Students are taught how music reflects and shapes
cultural, social, and technological contexts and the ethical responsibilities that
accompany music creation, performance, and analysis.

Music provides students with the knowledge and practices to create, perform,
analyse, evaluate, and communicate music in authentic contexts. They compose and
arrange music, perform individually and collaboratively, use music technologies for
notation and production, and develop research and analytical skills to interpret
musical works. Students also learn to communicate ideas to different audiences,
rehearse effectively, and make informed decisions that respect authorship, cultural
integrity, and professional practice.

As students progress through Year 11–13, they are taught to apply musical
knowledge with increasing independence, sophistication, and critical insight. Their
compositions, performances, analyses, and use of technology become more refined
and purposeful as they integrate theory, research, and reflective evaluation. This
progression enables students to make increasingly considered, individual, and
nuanced creative and interpretive decisions, adapting their knowledge and skills to a
wider range of musical contexts, audiences, and purposes.

 Disciplinary Writing

 Focus: the use of writing to reflect the ways in which knowledge is organised, analysed, and communicated within the discipline.
 In Music, students use explicitly taught disciplinary writing to record, explain, analyse, and justify musical concepts and decisions for specific purposes and users.

Performance requirements
The performance requirements of the Music curriculum assume a level of technical
proficiency in the chosen instrument(s) or vocally which aligns with 3 to 5 years of
sustained individual or group tuition. This should be factored into pathway planning,
noting that some students may not have had tuition previously.

Artificial intelligence (AI) can support learning, research, inquiry, and creative processes, but it may also introduce bias, inaccuracies, ethical concerns, and issues relating to
ownership. AI should enhance, not replace, critical or creative thinking, source evaluation, subject knowledge, or students’ own analysis and decision-making. Responsible AI use
emphasises the importance of exercising independent judgement, drawing on credible sources, verifying information, being transparent about AI use, considering diverse
perspectives, and developing independent thinking. In Music, where students use AI-assisted processes, they should critically evaluate and direct their use of those tools,
maintain ownership of creative decisions, and ensure that creative works reflect their own artistic intent, experimentation, and creative development.
